title: Databases
meta: This is a trigger file, not study material. Question visible → answer OUT LOUD (or write the query) → then expand → grade what you missed.

questions.text: Second-highest salary. Then the Nth.
points: Pattern: rank the distinct values, then filter on the rank

Query:
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) WHERE rnk = 2 LIMIT 1;
On the sample: salaries 300, 260, 250, 250… → 260
DENSE_RANK = Nth distinct value · ROW_NUMBER would count the tied 250s separately
No Nth value → empty result; wrap in a scalar subquery if they want NULL
questions.prompt: employees(id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hired_on)
questions.flow: dense-rank by salary → filter rank = N → one row
questions.trap: LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 with ties at the top
questions.practice: 176 Second Highest Salary · 177 Nth Highest Salary

questions.text: Top two earners in each department.
points: Pattern: number rows inside a partition, then filter outside

Query:
SELECT dept_id, name, salary FROM (
  SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM employees e
) WHERE rn <= 2;
On the sample: Eng → Asha 300, Dev 260 · Sales → Fay 220, Eli 200
ROW_NUMBER = exactly N rows · DENSE_RANK = N salary levels, ties kept
Add a tie-breaker to ORDER BY, or the result changes between runs
questions.prompt: employees(id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hired_on)
questions.flow: partition → order → number → filter in the outer query
questions.trap: filtering on a window function in the same WHERE
questions.practice: 185 Department Top Three Salaries · 184 Department Highest Salary

questions.text: Find duplicate emails. Then delete them, keeping one row each.
points: Pattern: group to find, keep MIN(id) per group to delete

Query:
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n FROM users
GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

DELETE FROM users
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM users GROUP BY email);
On the sample: a@x.com × 3 → after the delete, ids 1, 2, 5 remain
HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters rows before grouping
Then add a unique constraint, or the duplicates come back
Big table → delete in batches (Q45)
questions.flow: group + having → keep min id → delete the rest → unique constraint
questions.trap: cleaning up without fixing the write path
questions.practice: 182 Duplicate Emails · 196 Delete Duplicate Emails

questions.text: Running total of paid revenue, and a 3-order moving average.
points: Pattern: an aggregate with OVER (ORDER BY …) and an explicit frame

Query:
SELECT created_at, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) AS running_total,
  AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id
      ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_3
FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';
On the sample: amounts 100, 150, 300… → running 100, 250, 550 · avg_3 100, 125, 183.3
Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE … CURRENT ROW → ties are summed together
ROWS counts rows; RANGE groups equal sort keys
questions.flow: order → choose frame (ROWS) → aggregate over it
questions.trap: leaving the frame implicit when the sort key has ties
questions.practice: 1204 Last Person to Fit in the Bus · 1321 Restaurant Growth

questions.text: Employees who earn more than their manager.
points: Pattern: self-join: the same table twice, with two aliases

Query:
SELECT e.name, e.salary,
       m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
On the sample: Dev 260 > Bo 250 · Fay 220 > Eli 200
Inner join drops the CEO (manager_id NULL); LEFT JOIN keeps them
Index on manager_id if the hierarchy is large
questions.prompt: employees(id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hired_on)
questions.flow: alias employee + alias manager → join on manager_id → compare
questions.trap: forgetting the top of the tree has no manager
questions.practice: 181 Employees Earning More Than Their Managers

questions.text: Customers who have never placed an order.
points: Pattern: anti-join → NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN … IS NULL)

Query:
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
On the sample: Corex
Same data with NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) → zero rows
Why: one NULL in the list makes x NOT IN (…) evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row
NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and plans as an anti-join
questions.prompt:
customers(id, name)
orders(id, customer_id, amount, status, created_at)   -- customer_id can be NULL
questions.flow: anti-join → NOT EXISTS → check the subquery column for NULLs
questions.trap: NOT IN over a nullable column
questions.practice: 183 Customers Who Never Order

questions.text: Month-over-month revenue growth, in percent.
points: Pattern: aggregate to the period first, then LAG over the periods

Query:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT substr(created_at, 1, 7) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS growth_pct
FROM m;
On the sample: Jan 250 → Feb 300 (+20.0%) → Mar 520 (+73.3%)
First month → NULL growth, not 0
Postgres: date_trunc('month', created_at) · missing months need a calendar table
100.0, not 100: integer division truncates
questions.flow: group by month → LAG previous → (cur − prev) / prev
questions.trap: a month with no orders silently disappears from the series
questions.practice: 197 Rising Temperature · 1193 Monthly Transactions I

questions.text: Longest streak of consecutive login days per user.
points: Pattern: gaps and islands → date minus row number is constant inside a streak

Query:
WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins),
g AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
         julianday(login_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS grp
  FROM d
)
SELECT user_id, MAX(n) AS longest_streak FROM (
  SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS n FROM g
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
) GROUP BY user_id;
On the sample: user 1 (1–3 Mar, 7–8 Mar) → 3 · user 2 → 1
DISTINCT first: two logins on one day would break the arithmetic
Postgres: login_date - ROW_NUMBER()::int in place of julianday
questions.flow: dedupe days → date − row_number = island id → count per island → max
questions.trap: skipping the dedupe step
questions.practice: 180 Consecutive Numbers · 601 Human Traffic of Stadium

questions.text: One row per customer, with paid and refunded totals as columns.
points: Pattern: pivot by conditional aggregation

Query:
SELECT customer_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS paid,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
    AS refunded
FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY customer_id;
On the sample: customer 1 → 950 / 0 · customer 2 → 50 / 200
Postgres shorthand: SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')
Columns must be known up front; unknown categories → pivot in the application
questions.flow: group by the row key → one CASE-sum per output column
questions.trap: COUNT(CASE … ELSE 0 END) counts every row
questions.practice: 1179 Reformat Department Table · 1907 Count Salary Categories

questions.text: Median salary per department.
points: Pattern: number the rows, pick the middle one or two, average them

Query:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept_id, salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS n
  FROM employees
)
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS median FROM r
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
GROUP BY dept_id;
Odd n → both expressions give the same row · even n → the two middle rows
Postgres has it built in: percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)
questions.prompt: employees(id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hired_on)
questions.flow: row_number + count per group → middle positions → average
questions.trap: using AVG and calling it the median

questions.text: Latest record per user from a change log.
points: Pattern: top-1 per group → ROW_NUMBER … ORDER BY updated_at DESC, keep rn = 1

Query:
SELECT user_id, city FROM (
  SELECT p.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM profile_changes p
) WHERE rn = 1;
On the sample: user 1 → Pune · user 2 → Goa
Postgres shorthand: SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) … ORDER BY user_id, updated_at DESC
Equal timestamps → add a tie-breaker column
Index (user_id, updated_at DESC) makes it cheap
questions.flow: partition by key → order newest first → keep row 1
questions.trap: GROUP BY user_id with MAX(updated_at) and a non-aggregated city
questions.practice: 1164 Product Price at a Given Date

questions.text: Everyone who reports to a manager, directly or indirectly, with their depth.
points: Pattern: recursive CTE → anchor row, then join children to the previous level

Query:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, t.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id = t.id
)
SELECT depth, name FROM tree ORDER BY depth, id;
On the sample: 0 Asha · 1 Bo, Chen, Eli · 2 Dev, Fay, Gus
A cycle in the data → infinite recursion: cap depth, or track the path
Index on manager_id; each level is one join
questions.prompt: employees(id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hired_on)
questions.flow: anchor → recursive member joins to the CTE → stops when no rows are added
questions.trap: no guard against cycles

questions.text: Split each user's events into sessions: a new session after 30 minutes of inactivity.
points: Pattern: flag a boundary with LAG, then a running SUM of the flags = session id

Query:
WITH f AS (
  SELECT user_id, ts,
    CASE WHEN LAG(ts) OVER w IS NULL
           OR (julianday(ts) - julianday(LAG(ts) OVER w))
              * 1440 > 30
         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new
  FROM events
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)
)
SELECT user_id, ts,
  SUM(is_new) OVER (
    PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_no
FROM f;
On the sample: user 1 at 10:00, 10:10 → session 1 · 10:50, 11:05 → session 2
Postgres: ts - LAG(ts) OVER w > interval '30 minutes'
Same two-step shape solves any "start a new group when…" problem
questions.flow: LAG → gap > threshold? flag 1 → running sum of flags
questions.trap: trying to do it in one window pass

questions.text: Find overlapping bookings for a room, and the peak number at once.
points: Pattern: two intervals overlap when each starts before the other ends

Query:
SELECT a.id, b.id FROM bookings a JOIN bookings b
  ON a.room_id = b.room_id AND a.id < b.id
 AND a.start_ts < b.end_ts AND b.start_ts < a.end_ts;

WITH pts AS (SELECT start_ts AS t, 1 AS d FROM bookings
             UNION ALL SELECT end_ts, -1 FROM bookings)
SELECT MAX(running) AS peak
FROM (SELECT SUM(d) OVER (ORDER BY t, d) AS running FROM pts);
On the sample: pairs (1,2), (1,3), (2,3) · peak = 3
a.id < b.id → each pair once, no self-pairs
Peak = sweep line: +1 at a start, −1 at an end, running sum; ORDER BY t, d ends before starts at the same instant
To prevent overlaps: Postgres exclusion constraint on a range type
questions.flow: overlap test a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end → sweep line for the peak
questions.trap: checking only "b starts inside a"

questions.text: Day-1 retention by signup cohort.
points: Pattern: first event per user = cohort; then test for an event at cohort + N days

Query:
WITH first AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS d0
  FROM logins GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT f.d0 AS cohort, COUNT(*) AS users,
  SUM(EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM logins l
    WHERE l.user_id = f.user_id
      AND l.login_date = date(f.d0, '+1 day'))) AS back_day_1
FROM first f GROUP BY f.d0;
On the sample: cohort 1 Mar → 2 users, 1 back on day 1 (50%)
Postgres: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (…)) and d0 + 1
Say which definition: exactly day N, or on or after day N
Recent cohorts haven't had N days yet → exclude them
questions.flow: min date per user → cohort → exists on d0 + N → users back / cohort size
questions.trap: counting logins, not distinct users
questions.practice: 550 Game Play Analysis IV

questions.text: Write an idempotent upsert that never lets an older update overwrite a newer one.
points: Pattern: INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, guarded by a version or timestamp

Query:
INSERT INTO inventory(sku, qty, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?)
ON CONFLICT(sku) DO UPDATE
  SET qty = excluded.qty, updated_at = excluded.updated_at
  WHERE excluded.updated_at > inventory.updated_at;
On the sample: A1 at 1 Mar → apply 5 Mar (qty 9) → apply 2 Mar (qty 2) ignored → A1 stays 9
Replaying the same message changes nothing → safe for at-least-once delivery
Needs a unique constraint on the conflict target
MySQL: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE · SQL Server, Oracle: MERGE
questions.flow: insert → conflict on key → update only if the incoming row is newer
questions.trap: read-then-write in the application: a race between the two statements

questions.text: 📝 "Paginate a large table without OFFSET.
points: Pattern: keyset (seek) pagination → "rows after the last one I saw"

Query:
SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-03-01', 5)   -- last row seen
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 2;
On the sample: next page → (4, 14 Feb), (3, 3 Feb)
OFFSET n reads and discards n rows → page 10,000 is slow, and rows shift under concurrent inserts
Keyset is an index seek on (created_at, id): constant cost per page
Cost: no "jump to page 57"; the sort key must be unique → add id as a tie-breaker
questions.flow: order by (sort key, id) → pass the last row as a cursor → seek, limit
questions.trap: a non-unique sort key, which skips or repeats rows

questions.text: How does a B-tree index work, and when is it not used?
points: Sorted, balanced tree → O(log n) to find a key, then a range scan along the leaves
Good for: =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, prefix LIKE 'abc%'
Not used: function on the column (LOWER(email)), leading wildcard, implicit type cast
Not used: low selectivity → the planner prefers a scan to many random reads
Every index is paid for on every write
questions.flow: sorted tree → seek + range → skipped when the predicate isn't sargable or selective
questions.trap: "add an index" with no plan, no selectivity, no write cost

questions.text: Composite index on (customer_id, created_at). Which queries can use it?
points: Leftmost prefix: usable from the first column onward, in order
WHERE customer_id = 1 AND created_at > … → seek on both
WHERE created_at > … alone → full scan, the index can't be entered
Order rule: equality columns first, then the range column, then sort columns
Run on SQLite: first query → SEARCH … USING INDEX (customer_id=? AND created_at>?); second → SCAN orders
questions.flow: equality columns → one range column → anything after the range can't seek
questions.trap: ordering columns by "most selective first" regardless of the predicates

questions.text: What is a covering index?
points: The index holds every column the query needs → the table is never read
Plan shows an index-only scan (Postgres) / USING COVERING INDEX (SQLite, run)
Postgres: INCLUDE (col) adds payload columns without widening the key
Postgres caveat: needs the visibility map to be current, so vacuum matters
Cost: a wider index → more write work and more memory
questions.flow: query columns ⊆ index columns → no heap lookups → fewer random reads
questions.trap: SELECT * on a query you tried to cover

questions.text: Walk me through reading an EXPLAIN plan.
points: Read inside out: the deepest nodes run first
Per node: scan type (seq / index / index-only / bitmap), join type, estimated rows
EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds actual rows and time → estimate ≠ actual = stale statistics
Look for: a scan on a big table, a nested loop over many rows, a sort spilling to disk
Fix order: statistics → predicate shape → index → rewrite
questions.flow: find the costliest node → compare estimated vs actual rows → fix the cause
questions.trap: tuning from EXPLAIN without ANALYZE

questions.text: Isolation levels: which anomalies does each one allow?
points: Read uncommitted → dirty reads · Read committed → non-repeatable reads, phantoms
Repeatable read → standard allows phantoms · Serializable → none
Defaults differ: Postgres = read committed, MySQL InnoDB = repeatable read
Postgres repeatable read = snapshot isolation: no phantoms, but write skew remains
Serializable → transactions can abort → the application must retry
questions.flow: name the anomaly → the lowest level that prevents it → retry on serialization failure
questions.trap: assuming "repeatable read" means the same thing on every engine

questions.text: What is MVCC, and what does it cost?
points: Each write creates a new row version; readers see a snapshot
Readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers
Cost: dead versions pile up → vacuum (Postgres) or purge of undo (InnoDB)
A long-running transaction pins old versions → bloat, slower scans
Write–write conflicts still need locks or a first-committer-wins rule
questions.flow: versions per row → snapshot reads → garbage collection of dead versions
questions.trap: an idle-in-transaction session left open for hours

questions.text: How does a deadlock happen, and how do you prevent it?
points: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs → a cycle
The database detects it and aborts one victim
Prevent: take locks in a consistent order (e.g. sort ids before updating)
Keep transactions short; no user or network waits inside one
Always retry the victim; SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for queue workers
questions.flow: lock cycle → detector aborts one → fix lock order → retry
questions.trap: treating the deadlock error as fatal instead of retrying

questions.text: What does the write-ahead log give you?
points: Change is written to the log first, sequentially, and fsynced at commit
Durability: after a crash, replay the log → committed work survives
Data pages are flushed later, at a checkpoint → cheap sequential I/O up front
The same stream feeds replication and CDC
Knobs trade safety for speed: group commit, asynchronous commit
questions.flow: log record → fsync at commit → pages later → replay on crash
questions.trap: turning off fsync "for performance" on data you can't lose

questions.text: Nested loop, hash join, merge join: when does the planner pick each?
points: Nested loop: small outer side + an index on the inner → best for selective lookups
Hash join: large, unsorted inputs with an equality condition → build a hash, probe
Merge join: both inputs already sorted (or indexed) on the key
Hash needs memory → spills to disk when it doesn't fit
A bad choice usually means a bad row estimate
questions.flow: row estimates + available indexes + sort order → algorithm
questions.trap: forcing a join type instead of fixing the statistics

questions.text: 📝 "B-tree or LSM-tree?
points: B-tree: update in place → fast, predictable reads; random I/O on writes
LSM-tree: append to a memtable + log → flush to sorted files → compaction merges them
LSM wins on write-heavy workloads; reads may check several files (Bloom filters help)
Costs differ: B-tree → page splits, fragmentation · LSM → compaction I/O, space spikes
B-tree: Postgres, MySQL InnoDB · LSM: RocksDB, Cassandra, and many distributed stores
questions.flow: read-heavy + range scans → B-tree · write-heavy ingest → LSM + compaction budget
questions.trap: ignoring compaction when sizing an LSM store

questions.text: What is the N+1 query problem?
points: One query for the list, then one query per row for a related item
Usually an ORM's lazy loading inside a loop
Invisible in tests with 5 rows; N round trips in production
Fix: join fetch, or batch with WHERE id IN (…)
Detect: query count per request in traces or the ORM's log
questions.flow: list query → loop triggers a query per row → replace with a join or one IN query
questions.trap: "the query is fast": each one is, there are just 500 of them

questions.text: Why a connection pool, and how big?
points: A connection is expensive: Postgres starts a process per connection
Pool = a fixed set of reused connections; requests queue when it's full
Smaller is usually faster: start near 2 × CPU cores of the database, then measure
Pool size × app instances must stay under the database's connection limit
External pooler (PgBouncer, transaction mode) for many instances; session features don't carry over
questions.flow: fixed pool → queue instead of overload → size from DB cores, not app threads
questions.trap: raising the pool size when the database is the bottleneck

questions.text: SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually decide?
points: Start from access patterns and consistency needs, not from the product name
Relational: joins, ad-hoc queries, multi-row transactions, constraints
NoSQL: a known, narrow set of access patterns at very high scale; flexible or sparse records
You trade query flexibility for predictable scale
Default: one relational database until a measured limit says otherwise
questions.flow: list the queries → consistency needed → scale and shape → then pick
questions.trap: "NoSQL because it scales" with no access patterns written down

questions.text: Normalise or denormalise?
points: Normalise (to 3NF) → one fact in one place; no update anomalies
Denormalise → fewer joins on a hot read path; you now own keeping copies in sync
Do it for a measured read problem, not by default
Options before copying columns: an index, a materialised view, a cache
Record who updates the copy: trigger, application, or CDC
questions.flow: normalise first → measure the read path → denormalise the one hot query → own the sync
questions.trap: duplicated data with no owner for consistency

questions.text: Key-value, document, wide-column, graph: which fits what?
points: Key-value → lookup by key: sessions, caches, feature flags
Document → an aggregate read and written as a whole; varying fields
Wide-column → huge write volume, queries by partition key + sorted range
Graph → the question is about relationships: paths, neighbours, many hops
Most systems are polyglot: a relational core plus one or two specialised stores
questions.flow: shape of the query → model → each added store is another thing to operate
questions.trap: a document store used for heavily relational data

questions.text: UUID or auto-increment primary key?
points: Auto-increment: small, ordered → inserts append to the index; but one generator, and ids are guessable
Random UUID (v4): generated anywhere; inserts land all over the B-tree → page splits, cache misses
Time-ordered ids (UUIDv7, ULID): distributed generation and index locality
Key size multiplies: every secondary index and foreign key carries it
Don't expose sequential ids publicly if enumeration matters
questions.flow: need distributed generation? → time-ordered id · single writer → bigint
questions.trap: random UUIDs as the clustered key of a write-heavy table

questions.text: Optimistic or pessimistic locking?
points: Optimistic: read a version, write WHERE version = ?; zero rows updated → someone else won → retry
Pessimistic: SELECT … FOR UPDATE → others wait
Optimistic fits rare conflicts and long think time (a user editing a form)
Pessimistic fits frequent conflicts on short critical sections (decrementing stock)
Never hold a database lock across a user interaction
questions.flow: conflict rate low → version check + retry · high → lock briefly
questions.trap: read–modify–write with neither

questions.text: Row store or column store?
points: Row store (OLTP): whole rows together → fast point reads and writes
Column store (OLAP): each column together → scans a few columns of billions of rows
Columnar compresses well and skips columns and blocks the query doesn't need
Columnar is poor at single-row updates
Usual shape: OLTP database → CDC or batch → warehouse
questions.flow: many small transactions → row · few big aggregations → column
questions.trap: running analytics on the primary OLTP database at peak

questions.text: Cache-aside, write-through or write-behind?
points: Cache-aside: read cache → miss → read DB → fill; on write, delete the key
Write-through: write the cache and DB together → fresh cache, slower writes
Write-behind: write the cache, flush later → fast, and can lose data
Every cache needs a TTL as a backstop for missed invalidations
Hot key expires → stampede: use a lock or early refresh
questions.flow: cache-aside by default → invalidate on write → TTL backstop → stampede guard
questions.trap: updating the cache instead of deleting it, and racing a concurrent write

questions.text: Partitioning, replication, sharding: which problem does each solve?
points: Partitioning (one node): a big table split by range or hash → pruning, cheap drops of old data
Replication: copies of all data → read scale and availability; not write scale
Sharding: data split across nodes → write scale and size; cross-shard queries get hard
Order to try: indexes and queries → cache → read replicas → partition → shard
Sharding is the hardest one to undo
questions.flow: read problem → replicas · big-table problem → partition · write or size ceiling → shard
questions.trap: "the database is slow, so we shard"

questions.text: A query that took 20 ms now takes 4 s. Nothing was deployed. Diagnose it.
points: Get the actual plan now (EXPLAIN ANALYZE) and compare with the old one
Plan flip: stale statistics or data growth pushed the planner to a different join or scan
Data skew: one customer or value became huge → the same plan is now wrong for it
Contention: lock waits or I/O saturation, not the query itself → check wait events
Bloat or a dropped/invalid index
Fix the cause: analyse, index, rewrite; pin a plan only as a stopgap
questions.flow: actual plan → estimated vs actual rows → plan flip, skew, or waiting? → fix that
questions.trap: adding an index before looking at the plan

questions.text: A user saves a change and doesn't see it on the next page. Why?
points: The read went to a replica that hasn't applied the write yet: replication lag
Asynchronous replication → replicas are eventually consistent
Fix for the user: read-your-writes → route that user to the primary for a short window, or wait for the replica to reach the write's log position
Synchronous replication removes it, at the cost of write latency
Monitor lag in seconds and in bytes; alert on it
questions.flow: write to primary → read from a lagging replica → pin recent writers to the primary
questions.trap: sending every read to replicas with no rule for recent writes

questions.text: 📝 "Add a NOT NULL column to a 500 GB table with zero downtime.
points: Expand → backfill → contract; never one big blocking statement
Add the column nullable (a metadata change on modern engines)
Backfill in small batches, each its own transaction, throttled by replica lag
Application writes the new column first (dual-write), then reads it
Add the constraint last: Postgres → CHECK … NOT VALID, then VALIDATE
Set a lock timeout: a DDL waiting for a lock blocks everyone queued behind it
questions.flow: add nullable → deploy writers → backfill in batches → validate constraint → drop old
questions.trap: one UPDATE of the whole table inside a single transaction

questions.text: One shard is hot while the others idle. What now?
points: Cause: a skewed key → one tenant, one celebrity, or a time-based key where "now" is one shard
Short term: cache the hot key, rate-limit the hot tenant, move it to its own shard
Long term: a better key → add a suffix or hash to spread it, or a composite key
A directory (lookup) layer lets you move individual tenants
Measure per-key traffic before choosing; averages hide the skew
questions.flow: find the hot key → isolate or cache it now → change the key or add a directory
questions.trap: adding more shards when one key is the whole problem

questions.text: The database hits max connections under load.
points: Count first: pool size × instances vs the database limit
Autoscaling the app multiplies connections exactly when the database is struggling
Leaks: connections not returned; transactions left idle in transaction
Fix: smaller pools + an external pooler; timeouts on idle transactions
Slow queries hold connections longer → fix them and the "connection" problem shrinks
questions.flow: instances × pool vs limit → find leaks and long holders → pooler + timeouts
questions.trap: raising max_connections and making every query slower

questions.text: Deadlocks spike after a release.
points: Read the deadlock report: it names both statements and the locks
New code path updates the same rows in a different order
Or a new index / foreign key added a lock the old path didn't take
Batch jobs touching many rows in arbitrary order → sort by key first
Until fixed: retries with backoff keep users whole
questions.flow: deadlock log → the two statements → make lock order consistent → retry as the net
questions.trap: raising lock timeouts

questions.text: Rows are being deleted, but the table keeps growing.
points: MVCC: a delete marks a version dead; space is reused only after cleanup
Postgres: autovacuum can't keep up, or is blocked by a long transaction or stale replication slot
Vacuum makes space reusable; it rarely returns it to the OS
Fix: find and end the old transaction; tune autovacuum for that table
Shrink for real: an online rebuild tool, or partition and drop old partitions
questions.flow: dead versions → cleanup blocked or too slow → unblock + tune → rebuild if needed
questions.trap: VACUUM FULL on a live table: it takes an exclusive lock

questions.text: Delete 200 million old rows from a live table.
points: Never one statement: huge transaction, long locks, log and replica lag explode
Batches of a few thousand by key range, commit each, pause on replica lag
Better: partition by time and DROP the old partition → instant, no bloat
If you're keeping only a small part: copy the keepers to a new table and swap
Check foreign keys and triggers: each deleted row may fan out
questions.flow: partitioned? drop the partition · else batch by key range, throttled
questions.trap: DELETE … WHERE created_at < … in one transaction at midday

questions.text: 📝 "What are RPO and RTO, and how do you know your backups work?
points: RPO = how much data you can lose · RTO = how long recovery may take
Full backups + continuous log archiving → point-in-time recovery, RPO of seconds to minutes
A replica is not a backup: a bad DELETE replicates too
A backup is unproven until restored: schedule restore drills and time them
Keep copies in another account and region; test the decryption keys
questions.flow: set RPO/RTO with the business → base backup + log archive → restore drill → measure
questions.trap: "we have replicas, so we're covered"

questions.text: Explain CAP and PACELC with real systems.
points: CAP: during a network partition, choose consistency or availability; you can't have both
No partition → CAP says nothing → PACELC: else, trade latency against consistency
CP-leaning: a single-leader relational database, consensus stores → refuse writes without a quorum
AP-leaning: Dynamo-style stores → accept writes, reconcile later
Often tunable per request (quorum settings); the choice is per operation, not per company
questions.flow: partition → C or A · normal operation → latency or consistency → decide per operation
questions.trap: "we chose CA"

questions.text: Choose a shard key for a multi-tenant SaaS.
points: Goals: most queries hit one shard, load spreads evenly, the key never changes
tenant_id → queries stay local; risk: one giant tenant = a hot shard
Mitigate: a directory that maps tenants to shards → big tenants get their own
Hash of the key spreads load; range keeps ranges together but hot-spots on "latest"
Cross-shard joins and transactions become the application's problem → design them out
questions.flow: list the queries → key that keeps each on one shard → check skew → directory for outliers
questions.trap: sharding on an auto-increment id or a timestamp

questions.text: Save an order and publish an event. How do you keep them consistent?
points: The dual-write problem: DB commit and message publish can't be atomic → one can fail
Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay or CDC publishes it
Delivery is at-least-once → consumers must be idempotent
2PC gives atomicity across systems; it blocks on coordinator failure and few brokers support it
Saga: a chain of local transactions with compensating actions for multi-service flows
questions.flow: one local transaction (data + outbox row) → relay publishes → idempotent consumer
questions.trap: publish, then commit (or commit, then publish) and hope

questions.text: How does change data capture work, and what do you use it for?
points: Reads the database's log (WAL / binlog) and emits each committed change in order
No dual writes, low load on the source, nothing missed between polls
Uses: search index, cache invalidation, warehouse loads, the outbox relay
You own: schema evolution, ordering per key, replays, and the initial snapshot
Postgres: a stalled consumer holds its replication slot → the log piles up on the primary
questions.flow: log → connector → stream (ordered per key) → idempotent consumers
questions.trap: polling updated_at and missing deletes

questions.text: Quorums: what do N, R and W buy you?
points: N replicas · a write waits for W acks · a read asks R replicas
R + W > N → every read overlaps the latest write → strong-ish consistency
N=3, W=2, R=2 → survives one node down for reads and writes
W=1, R=1 → fastest, and stale reads are possible
Still needs conflict handling: last-write-wins loses data on clock skew
questions.flow: pick N → set R and W per operation → R + W > N for read-after-write
questions.trap: assuming a quorum makes operations transactional

questions.text: Model data for a DynamoDB- or Cassandra-style store.
points: Access patterns first: list every query before any table
Partition key → which node and what's stored together · sort key → order within the partition
One query = one partition read; no joins → denormalise and duplicate on purpose
Keep partitions bounded: a key that grows forever becomes a hot, huge partition
A new access pattern can mean a new table or index → cost of flexibility is paid up front
questions.flow: queries → partition key per query → sort key for ranges → duplicate data per pattern
questions.trap: designing entities first, like a relational schema

questions.text: Multi-tenant data: shared tables, schema per tenant, or database per tenant?
points: Shared tables + tenant_id: cheapest, easiest to operate; isolation depends on every query
Schema per tenant: stronger separation; migrations × number of tenants
Database per tenant: best isolation and per-tenant restore; highest cost
Enforce in the database: row-level security or a mandatory tenant filter, not convention
Often tiered: shared for small tenants, dedicated for large or regulated ones
questions.flow: isolation and compliance need → cost per tenant → tier → enforce below the application
questions.trap: tenant isolation by remembering a WHERE clause

questions.text: Where do vectors go: in Postgres with pgvector, or a dedicated vector store?
points: pgvector: one system, transactional with your rows, SQL filters and joins on metadata
Fits up to millions of vectors and moderate query rates; measure recall and latency
Dedicated store: very large scale, heavy filtered search, index tuning as a product
Cost of a second store: sync, consistency and another thing to operate
Decide on scale, filter selectivity and who operates it
questions.flow: start in the database you have → measure recall and p95 → move when a limit is hit
questions.trap: a separate vector store on day one for ten thousand documents

questions.text: Scale NL-to-SQL when the database has hundreds of tables.
points: The whole schema won't fit, and wrong joins rise with every table shown
Retrieve the schema: index table and column descriptions, pass only the relevant few
A semantic layer: governed metrics and approved views, not raw tables
Safety: read-only role, row-level security, SELECT only, time and scan limits
Evaluate by result, on golden business questions, not by SQL text

links.label: data and sql analyst agents
links.target: 03-Agentic-AI/12-Applied & Domain Patterns/108-data and sql analyst agents

questions.flow: question → retrieve relevant schema → generate over curated views → limits → check result
questions.trap: pasting the full schema into the prompt

questions.text: Tell me about a database problem you diagnosed in production.
points: Open with the symptom and its cost: memory, latency, restarts
How you found it: the plan, the slow-query log, a heap or row-count check
The cause in one line → e.g. a Cartesian product in a matching query (S4 in the story bank)
The fix and the guard you added: a constraint, an alert, a test
<fill: the system, how you found it, the number before → after>
questions.flow: symptom → evidence → cause → fix → guard → number
questions.trap: "we added an index and it got faster"
